name: greek yogurt lemon pound cake
instructions:
Captured from a baking book (loaf cakes chapter, page 83 — author not identified in the excerpt). Explicitly a POUND CAKE, not a french yogurt cake — different format, different yogurt type, different fat, different technique. See notes on how it compares to french-yogurt-cake.

MAKES ONE 9x5-INCH LOAF CAKE.

=== INGREDIENTS ===

- 4 oz (113g) COLD unsalted butter, cubed, + more for buttering the pan
- 1 cup (200g) granulated sugar, + more for coating the pan
- 4 tbsp (24g) grated LEMON ZEST
- 2 cups (250g) unbleached all-purpose flour
- 1 tsp (4g) baking powder
- 1/2 tsp (3g) baking soda
- 1/2 tsp (1.5g) Diamond Crystal kosher salt
- 2 large eggs (100g)
- 1 1/2 cups (360g) plain FULL-FAT GREEK YOGURT

=== PROCEDURE ===

1. PREPARE THE PAN: generously butter a 9x5-inch loaf pan and coat the inside with sugar.
2. MAKE LEMON SUGAR: combine the 1 cup granulated sugar with the lemon zest in a small bowl. Rub the zest into the sugar with your fingers until the sugar is bright yellow and fragrant.
3. In the bowl of a stand mixer fitted with the paddle attachment, mix the flour, baking powder, baking soda, lemon sugar, and salt together — this disperses the soda and powder and breaks up sugar lumps. Add the cold butter and mix on low speed until the mixture resembles rustic sand, ~4 min.
4. Whisk the eggs and greek yogurt together in a small bowl. Slowly add to the butter-flour mixture on low speed. Mix until everything is combined and no dry flour remains.
5. Transfer batter to the prepared pan. Tap the pan on the counter a few times to burst air pockets.
6. COLD OVEN START: place the cake into a TOTALLY COLD oven on the center rack. THEN turn the oven on to 350°F (176°C). See notes on why this technique matters.
7. Bake until a toothpick or wooden skewer inserted in the center comes out with a few moist crumbs clinging (50 min to 1 hour). Cake will be tall, puffy, browned at the edges.
8. Cool in the pan for 30 min before removing. Cool completely before cutting.

KEEPS: well wrapped in plastic or in a sealed container for up to 1 week.
notes:
=== HEADNOTE (FROM SOURCE) ===

Using greek yogurt in pound cake creates a perfect sturdy but tender crumb. Cake narrowly walks the line between sweet and savory — a nice alternative to a super-rich and sweet traditional pound cake. Source's favorite serving: with olive-oil ice cream and roasted figs.

=== HOW THIS DIFFERS FROM THE FRENCH YOGURT CAKE (SEE french-yogurt-cake) ===

This is NOT the same cake as the french-yogurt-cake in this cookbook. Several axes of difference — worth spelling out because the two are close enough to confuse:

1. FORMAT — POUND CAKE (LOAF), NOT ROUND CAKE: 9x5 loaf pan, sturdier, denser crumb. French yogurt cake is round, softer, more tender. Pound cake reads as a slice-and-serve loaf; french yogurt cake reads as a rustic frosted round.

2. YOGURT TYPE — GREEK (SPECIFICALLY), NOT PLAIN: greek yogurt is the load-bearing choice here — its thickness and higher protein give the pound cake its 'sturdy but tender' crumb. In the french-yogurt-cake, plain yogurt is preferred and greek is a fallback because plain gives the softer tender result THAT recipe wants. Same ingredient (yogurt), opposite role.

3. FAT — COLD BUTTER, NOT OIL: cold cubed butter incorporated into the dry ingredients like a pie dough. French yogurt cake uses oil (with butter as a secondary variant). Butter here gives the pound-cake density; oil in the french yogurt cake gives the softer round-cake tenderness.

4. LEAVENING — BAKING POWDER + BAKING SODA (BOTH): french yogurt cake uses baking powder only (2 tsp standard / 1.5 tsp butter variant). Greek pound cake uses baking powder AND baking soda (the soda reacts with greek yogurt's acidity for a specific lift the powder alone doesn't provide).

5. SUGAR TECHNIQUE — RUBBED INTO LEMON ZEST FIRST (LEMON SUGAR): rub the zest into the granulated sugar with your fingers until the sugar is bright yellow and fragrant. This releases the citrus oils into the sugar so they distribute through the entire cake. French yogurt cake just adds lemon zest to the batter directly; the lemon-sugar-rub technique is specific to this pound cake.

6. EGG COUNT — 2, NOT 3: fewer eggs, denser crumb. French yogurt cake uses 3 eggs.

7. BAKE METHOD — COLD OVEN START: place the cake in a TOTALLY COLD oven, then turn it on. Takes longer to bake but produces a wonderfully even, golden exterior (per source). French yogurt cake goes into a preheated 350°F oven. Different technique, different exterior result.

8. FLAVOR REGISTER — 'SWEET AND SAVORY' (SOURCE'S OWN FRAMING): the greek pound cake explicitly walks the line between sweet and savory — less rich, less sweet than a traditional pound cake, more suited to something like the source's olive-oil-ice-cream-and-figs pairing. French yogurt cake is squarely a sweet dessert with fruit or berry toppings.

WHEN TO REACH FOR WHICH: pound cake for a sturdier slice-and-serve loaf that pairs with something more savory-adjacent (olive oil ice cream, roasted figs, cheese course); french yogurt cake when you want a softer round cake with frosting and berry topping for a proper dessert format.

=== THE MORE INTERESTING DIFFERENCE — PROTEIN BALANCE ===

The eight technical axes above matter, but the more interesting angle: PROTEIN BALANCE. And it IS a balance — the recipe pulls in both directions rather than just cranking the protein dial:

PUSHING PROTEIN UP:
- GREEK YOGURT itself is meaningfully higher protein than plain (roughly 2x per volume).
- QUANTITY of yogurt is 3x: 1.5 cups here vs 1/2 cup in the french yogurt cake.

PULLING PROTEIN DOWN (compensating):
- FEWER EGGS: 2 vs 3 in the french yogurt cake.
- MORE FLOUR: 2 cups vs 1.5 cups.
- BUTTER (a non-protein ingredient) added on top of the fat structure.

NET: the pound cake ends up somewhat higher protein but not dramatically so. The greek yogurt's extra protein density is partially offset by fewer eggs and more flour/butter — the ratios have been reworked around greek yogurt's structural properties, not just its protein content. If you want to lean into protein density, the french yogurt cake's high-protein path (greek + 3 eggs + nuts + more yogurt) is actually a real competitor here despite the pound cake looking obviously protein-forward on the ingredient list.

=== COLD OVEN TECHNIQUE — WHY IT MATTERS ===

Source's technique: put the cake in a totally cold oven, close the door, THEN turn the oven on. The slow ramp-up as the oven preheats gives the cake time to set gradually rather than hitting a full 350°F all at once. Result per source: wonderfully even golden color on the outside, taller and puffier finished loaf.

Takes a little longer to bake (~50-60 min total from cold-start vs a shorter preheated-oven time). Plan for the extra time.

=== LEMON SUGAR RUB TECHNIQUE ===

Rub 4 tbsp grated lemon zest into 1 cup granulated sugar with your fingers until the sugar turns bright yellow and fragrant. This is a real technique step, not window-dressing — the sugar granules physically release the citrus oils from the zest through the abrasion, and the lemon-infused sugar then distributes through the entire cake. Skip the rub and just dump the zest into the batter and you get a less-cohesive lemon flavor.

=== COLD BUTTER, INCORPORATED LIKE PIE DOUGH ===

The cold butter goes in cubed and gets worked into the dry ingredients until the mixture looks like 'rustic sand.' This is closer to a pie-dough or scone technique than a cake technique — the fat coats the flour particles before liquid goes in, creating the sturdy-but-tender pound cake crumb rather than the airy-fluffy crumb you'd get from creaming softened butter with sugar.

=== KEEPS UP TO 1 WEEK — GENUINE MAKE-AHEAD DESSERT ===

Source notes: 1 week wrapped in plastic or sealed container. The pound cake format holds up much better than a frosted round cake would — worth planning around if you need something baked in advance.

=== SIBLING RECIPES ===

- french-yogurt-cake: the plain-yogurt round-cake sibling (see comparison note above). Different format, different technique, different serving register. Not interchangeable.
- chocolate-cake: Sally's triple chocolate cake (also uses buttermilk-or-yogurt). Different cake entirely; noted for completeness.
